title: Chesterton's gratitude
hookLine: Chesterton wonders why we give thanks before meals and not before plays and walks
tomorrow: how do you start the morning after something went wrong?

lines: BEFORE A PEN DIPPED IN INK?
cards: Steam off a plate, forks already lifting, and someone at the table says, wait. Grace before dinner is familiar. But grace before a concert?
Before a swim, a walk, a dance, before dipping a pen in ink? G. K.
Chesterton, an English writer who loved a paradox, jotted that very question in a notebook. Why save thanks for food?

teach.b: Chesterton's notebook line runs like a list. You say grace before meals, he writes. All right.

But he says grace before the concert and the play, before opening a book, before sketching, swimming, walking, playing, dancing, and before dipping the pen in the ink. The list keeps going because the gifts keep going.
In his book Orthodoxy he gives the reason: “The test of all happiness is gratitude.” Then he asks a child's question, the one to tell a friend tonight.
Children are grateful when Santa Claus puts toys and sweets in their stockings.
Couldn't he be grateful, he asks, for the gift of two miraculous legs to put in the stockings? Legs, a walk, a voice, a morning: things that never feel like gifts because they were always there.
For Chesterton, wonder comes before thanks. Nobody thanks anyone for what they've stopped noticing. Paul says it in one line to the Thessalonians: “In every thing give thanks.”
In every thing, not only at the table.
So Chesterton's grace isn't a longer prayer. It's a wider one. The meal is just where the habit starts.
A walk, a book or a song can get the same small pause before it begins.

how: Christians who say grace before meals sometimes widen the habit, as Chesterton did, and give thanks before walks, work, reading or music too.

o: a thank-you letter an author wrote to his readers
Chesterton's thanks before far more than meals
a short prayer said only at the start of a meal

games.q: where the thanks goes — tap the pairs.
p: the test of all happiness is gratitude

s: Chesterton thought grace before meals was a waste of time
'all right,' he says. he wants more graces, not fewer.
Chesterton asks why not be grateful for the legs in the stocking
children thank Santa for toys; he wants to give thanks for two miraculous legs.
giving thanks in every thing was Chesterton's own idea
Paul wrote it to the Thessalonians: in every thing give thanks.

games.q: your grandma says grace before her morning walk, and your cousin laughs: "it's not a meal!" which reply fits Chesterton?
o: a walk is a gift too; he said grace before walks, swims and books.
she's mixed up; grace only belongs at the table.
she's praying to stay safe on the walk, which isn't really thanks.
games.why: Chesterton wanted grace before the concert, the play, the walk and the pen. the meal is just where the habit starts.

practice: Stand up, and before the first step, pause to give thanks for what's about to carry you: two legs, a floor, the air. Then walk slowly for a minute, across the room or down a hall, feeling each foot land.
Come back, sit, and stay with the feeling of your feet on the ground.

wordCard.voice: Chesterton's gratitude. Thanks that doesn't wait for dinner: grace before a walk, a book, a pen dipped in ink.

carryVoice: Carry this: thanks before everything. The meal is just where the habit starts. Until tomorrow.
